clinicalPearls: Sickle cell disease is a clinical/haematologic phenotype caused by an assortment of genotypes; sickle cell anaemia (HbSS, homozygosity for the HbS Glu6Val mutation) is the most common, followed by HbSC disease (compound heterozygosity for HbS and HbC) and the HbS-beta thalassaemias (p.772).
The chief presenting symptom is pain: a hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis) in young children, and typical acute painful episodes in older children and adults (p.772).

Acute painful episodes are the most common acute events; pain is typically unprovoked, severe, in extremities or torso, often symmetrical and stereotypical for each patient, and lasts days to weeks (p.773).

In HbSC disease and HbS-beta+ thalassaemia, acute vaso-occlusive episodes occur at about half the rate of sickle cell anaemia and complications develop later; rarely such patients are asymptomatic (p.772).

Complications fall into two related groups: those driven by sickle vaso-occlusion (pain, acute chest syndrome, osteonecrosis, splenic infarction) and those driven by intravascular haemolysis (stroke, pulmonary/systemic vasculopathy, nephropathy, leg ulcers, gallstones, priapism); vaso-occlusive complications respond best to HbF induction (p.772-773).

Carriers of sickle cell trait (HbAS) outnumber patients with disease ~25 to 1; trait is usually benign with normal life expectancy, but carries a small risk of sudden death from heat-related exertional rhabdomyolysis and complications such as haematuria, papillary necrosis, hyposthenuria, splenic infarction at altitude and increased VTE risk (p.772, 775).

Autosplenectomy from repeated childhood splenic infarction is usual in sickle cell anaemia; a palpable spleen after age 5 suggests a coexisting genotype (e.g. thalassaemia or HbC) (p.769-770 reference and Table 103-2).

Hydroxyurea (acting mainly by inducing HbF) is standard of care for all patients with sickle cell anaemia and HbS-beta0 thalassaemia regardless of symptoms; in adults it roughly halves pain and acute chest syndrome and reduced mortality by 49% over 17.5 years (p.775).

Cure is possible with HLA-identical related-donor allogeneic stem cell transplant (event-free survival >95%, though only ~15% of patients have a fully matched donor) and with two approved ex vivo autologous gene therapies (lentiviral betaT87Q HbA gene; CRISPR/Cas9 disruption of the BCL11A enhancer) (p.775-776).
harrison.pathophysiology: HbS behaves like HbA except that it polymerises when deoxygenated: contacts between beta6 valine residues of deoxy-HbS and beta/alpha-globin residues form hemoglobin fascicles that injure the sickle erythrocyte, after a delay between initiation of polymerisation and accumulation of damaging polymer. Polymerisation depends on roughly the 30th power of hemoglobin concentration, so small changes in concentration or cell dehydration have large effects. Membrane vesiculation/microparticle release, activation of dehydrating channels (Gardos, K/Cl cotransport, Psickle) which raise mean corpuscular HbS concentration and reduce deformability, translocation of phosphatidylserine to the outer membrane leaflet, and oxidation produce irreversibly sickled cells (ISCs) that remain deformed regardless of oxygenation. Sickle erythrocytes adhere to endothelium and other blood cells, occluding small and large vessels (vaso-occlusion), and survive <20 days (normal ~120), haemolysing intra- and extravascularly. Intravascular haemolysis depletes haptoglobin and hemopexin and liberates heme, arginase and other DAMPs which scavenge nitric oxide, activate platelets and endothelium, reduce antioxidant activity, cause vasoconstriction and drive inflammation (p.772-774).
infectionMimics: Acute chest syndrome (pneumonia-like illness with chest pain, cough, fever, hypoxia and a pulmonary infiltrate) closely resembles and may coexist with bacterial pneumonia; antibiotics are almost always used even though a causative bacterium is often not cultured (p.775).
Multiorgan failure accompanying severe acute chest syndrome is often confused with, and can coexist with, sepsis (p.774, Table 103-3).
additionalInvestigations: High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and hemoglobin electrophoresis to quantify hemoglobin fractions (HbS, HbF, HbA, HbA2, HbC) and distinguish trait, sickle cell anaemia and HbSC disease (Table 103-2, Fig. 103-4, p.772).

Peripheral blood film: irreversibly sickled cells, target cells and nucleated red cells in HbSS/HbS-beta0 thalassaemia; HbC crystals, taco-folded cells and contracted microspherocytes in HbSC disease (Fig. 103-4, p.772-774).
DNA-based diagnosis for genetic counselling and family planning; antenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or cell-free DNA (p.772, 776).
Transcranial Doppler screening in children (ages 2-16) to identify stroke risk (Table 103-3, p.776).
Echocardiographic measurement of tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity (TRV) annually to screen for pulmonary hypertension.
Screening for microalbuminuria from age 10 for nephropathy, and annual fluorescein angiography from age 10 for retinopathy.
redFlags: Acute chest syndrome - chest pain, cough, fever, hypoxia and a pulmonary infiltrate; can be devastating with multilobar involvement, severe hypoxia, ARDS, multiorgan failure and rapid death (often from embolised necrotic marrow) (p.775).
Splenic sequestration (acute anemic episode) - rapid drop in hemoglobin; recurrent episodes are an indication for splenectomy (Table 103-3, p.774).
Aplastic crisis from parvovirus B19 infection causing acute worsening of anaemia with reticulocytopenia (Table 103-3, p.774; reticulocytopenia in acute worsening noted elsewhere).

Stroke and silent infarction - occur in 10-15% of cases, from early childhood into adulthood, with neurocognitive abnormalities even without apparent stroke; haemorrhagic stroke in adults (Table 103-3, p.773).

Functional/anatomic asplenia (autosplenectomy) places patients at high risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated organisms, notably overwhelming pneumococcal disease (p.776, 769/Table; pneumococcal chapter p.999).

Sudden unexpected death shortly after admission for acute pain (possible arrhythmia or pulmonary embolism); thrombocytopenia, leukocytosis >20,000 and rapidly developing acute anaemia portend severe acute chest syndrome and multiorgan failure (p.773, 775).
Multiorgan failure - can accompany severe acute chest syndrome, affecting CNS, liver, muscle, lung and kidney (Table 103-3, p.774).
harrison.prognosis: In the United States childhood death is now rare and the median age of death in sickle cell anaemia is in the fifth or sixth decade; by contrast in high-burden regions such as Nigeria most affected newborns die before age 5. Hydroxyurea reduced mortality by 49% over 17.5 years of follow-up. Genotype modifies severity: HbSC disease and HbS-beta+ thalassaemia have about half the complication rate of HbSS, and coexistent alpha thalassaemia (present in ~30% of HbSS) is associated with fewer strokes and leg ulcers and less pulmonary vascular and renal disease. Allogeneic transplantation and gene therapy offer potential cure (p.772, 775-776).
pitfalls: No diagnostic test can confirm or refute an acute pain episode; physical examination is often unhelpful and the presence of ISCs and the reticulocyte count are of no diagnostic value (p.773).

Supplemental oxygen is unnecessary unless hypoxia is present, and NSAIDs add little once intravenous opioids are given; overhydration and excessive opioids can compound dyspnoea and hypoxia in acute chest syndrome (p.773, 775).

Opioids should not be dosed on an 'as-needed' schedule - patient-controlled or fixed scheduled dosing with rescue doses is preferred, with monitoring to avoid excessive sedation; many patients are opioid-tolerant and need higher doses (p.773).
Transfusions are both overutilised and underutilised; they should usually be avoided in acute pain episodes and for stable chronic anaemia (p.776).
A palpable spleen after age 5 in sickle cell disease suggests a coexisting genotype rather than simple HbSS (p.769-770).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is largely defined by genotype: sickle cell trait (HbAS, usually benign); sickle cell anaemia (HbSS, vaso-occlusion- and haemolysis-related complications, Hb ~7-10 g/dL); HbS-beta0 thalassaemia (complication rate similar to HbSS); HbS-beta+ thalassaemia (~half the rate of HbSS depending on percent HbA); HbSC disease (near-asymptomatic to as severe as HbSS, ~half the complication rate, increased retinopathy risk); HbSE (resembles HbS-beta+ thalassaemia, often Asian/Indian ancestry); and HbSS-alpha thalassaemia (phenocopies HbS-beta0 thalassaemia with fewer strokes/leg ulcers and less pulmonary/renal disease). HbF level (influenced by HbS haplotype) modifies severity (p.772).
management: Hydroxycarbamide to induce foetal haemoglobin and reduce vaso-occlusive crises, acute chest syndrome and mortality, as the disease-modifying mainstay
Prompt management of acute painful crises with analgesia including opioids, together with rehydration and oxygenation
Infection prevention with penicillin prophylaxis and pneumococcal and other vaccination given functional hyposplenism, plus urgent treatment of febrile illness
Red-cell transfusion or exchange transfusion for acute chest syndrome, stroke and other severe complications, with a chronic transfusion programme for stroke prevention
Transcranial Doppler screening in children to identify those needing transfusion for primary stroke prevention
Surveillance for chronic complications including retinopathy, pulmonary hypertension via tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity, nephropathy with microalbuminuria screening, priapism and leg ulcers
Allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation and emerging gene therapy as curative options for severe disease, alongside folic acid supplementation
Genetic counselling with cascade and antenatal screening, and coordinated multidisciplinary specialist care
